questions.text: What is an argument (or logical deduction) in propositional logic?
options: A) A single statement that is always true.
B) An assertion that a given set of premises (hypotheses) yields a conclusion.
C) A single proposition that is false.
questions.correct_answer: B) An assertion that a given set of premises (hypotheses) yields a conclusion.
questions.explanation: The module states: 'An argument (logical deduction) is an assertion that a given set of statements p₁, p₂, ..., pₙ, called hypotheses or premises, yield another statement Q, called the conclusion.' Options A, C, and D are not definitions of an argument.

questions.text: When is an argument form considered valid?
options: A) If the conclusion is always false.
B) If the conclusion is true whenever all the premises are true.
C) If the premises are always false.
D) If the conclusion is independent of the premises.
questions.correct_answer: B) If the conclusion is true whenever all the premises are true.
questions.explanation: The module states: 'An argument form p₁, ..., pₙ ⊢ Q is said to be valid if Q is true whenever all the premises p₁, ..., pₙ are true; otherwise, it is invalid.'

questions.text: What is the Modus Tollens rule of inference?
options: C) $p \Rightarrow q, q \Rightarrow r \vdash p \Rightarrow r$
questions.explanation: The module states: 'Modus Tollens: ¬q, p ⇒ q ⊢ ¬p.' Option A is Modus Ponens. Option C is Syllogism. Option D is Adjunction.

questions.text: What is the Principle of Syllogism?
options: B) $p \Rightarrow q, q \Rightarrow r \vdash p \Rightarrow r$
questions.correct_answer: B) $p \Rightarrow q, q \Rightarrow r \vdash p \Rightarrow r$
questions.explanation: The module states: 'Principle of Syllogism: p ⇒ q, q ⇒ r ⊢ p ⇒ r.' Option A is Modus Ponens. Option C is Modus Tollens. Option D is Adjunction.

questions.text: How can an argument form be proven valid using a truth table?
options: A) By checking if the conclusion is false when premises are true.
B) By checking if the statement $(p_1 \wedge p_2 \wedge ... \wedge p_n) \Rightarrow Q$ is a tautology.
C) By checking if the premises are always false.
D) By counting the number of rows in the truth table.
questions.correct_answer: B) By checking if the statement $(p_1 \wedge p_2 \wedge ... \wedge p_n) \Rightarrow Q$ is a tautology.
questions.explanation: The module states: 'The argument form p₁, ..., pₙ ⊢ Q is valid iff the statement (p₁ ∧ p₂ ∧ ... ∧ pₙ) ⇒ Q is a tautology.'

questions.text: What does Modus Ponens allow you to conclude from $p$ and $p \Rightarrow q$?
questions.explanation: The module states: 'Modus Ponens: p, p ⇒ q ⊢ q.' Option A would require Modus Tollens. Option B is incorrect. Option D would require Adjunction.

questions.text: Which rule of inference allows you to conclude $p \wedge q$ from $p$ and $q$?
questions.explanation: The module states: 'Principle of Adjunction: p, q ⊢ p ∧ q.' Option A is Modus Tollens. Option B is Syllogism. Option D is Constructive Dilemma.

questions.text: What is the Constructive Dilemma rule of inference?
options: A) $p \Rightarrow q, r \Rightarrow s, p \vee r \vdash q \vee s$
questions.correct_answer: A) $p \Rightarrow q, r \Rightarrow s, p \vee r \vdash q \vee s$
questions.explanation: The module states: 'Constructive Dilemma: (p ⇒ q) ∧ (r ⇒ s), p ∨ r ⊢ q ∨ s.' Option B is Modus Ponens. Option C is Modus Tollens. Option D is Adjunction.

questions.text: What is the conclusion of the following argument: $p \Rightarrow q, \neg q \vdash ?$
questions.explanation: This is the Modus Tollens rule of inference: ¬q, p ⇒ q ⊢ ¬p. Option A would be the invalid fallacy of affirming the consequent. Option C would require Modus Ponens. Option D would require Adjunction.

questions.text: What does the rule of Conditionalization state?
options: D) $p \Rightarrow q, q \Rightarrow r \vdash p \Rightarrow r$
questions.explanation: The module states: 'Principle of Conditionalization: p ⊢ q ⇒ p.' Option A is Modus Ponens. Option C is the Law of Contrapositive. Option D is Syllogism.
